q: בן 75, הופנה על ידי רופא המשפחה לביצוע בדיקת הדמיה (MRI) במסגרת בירור ירידה קוגניטיבית הדרגתית ומתמדת במהלך השנה האחרונה. ברקע – יתר לחץ דם, סוכרת מסוג 2, ניתוח תיקון שבר בירך שמאל לפני כשנה ושבר ביד ימין לאחר נפילה לפני חודשיים. אשתו מדווחת על הפרעות שליטה על סוגר השתן מאז הנפילה והשבר בירך שמאל. בבדיקת MRI: מה הטיפול האפשרי למטופל זה?
o: DOPICAR
RIVASTIGMINE (EXELON)
ניתוח VENTRICULO-PRITONEAL SHANT
קרינה לאזור הפריאטלי מימין
explanation:
Cognitive decline, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence raise suspicion for **normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)**. When surgery is selected, the source describes CSF diversion by shunt; gait is the symptom most often improved (Hazzard 8e, p. 876).

**A. Dopicar.** Wrong, levodopa treats dopamine-responsive parkinsonism. Hydrocephalus is among the conditions with poor levodopa response; medication does not correct the CSF-flow disorder (pp. 876, 940).
**B. Rivastigmine (Exelon).** Wrong, rivastigmine treats symptoms of degenerative dementia. The process considered here is impaired CSF flow or absorption, for which a shunt is described (pp. 876, 913).
**C. Ventriculoperitoneal shunt surgery.** Correct, this is the described surgical approach to divert CSF for better absorption. The source stresses variable response and operative risk, requiring individual assessment (p. 876).
**D. Radiation to the right parietal region.** Wrong, the described hydrocephalus treatment is CSF diversion. Radiation does not address that absorption problem, and no tumor diagnosis justifying it is presented; this is an application of the source's mechanism (p. 876).

Assuming the MRI shows **ventriculomegaly** consistent with NPH, the preferred treatment in this question is CSF diversion through a VP shunt. This diverts excess ventricular CSF to the peritoneal cavity and may significantly improve symptoms, especially gait disturbance (p. 876; conditional application to the scenario).
NPH is a potentially reversible cause of cognitive decline, but cognitive improvement after shunting is not guaranteed (p. 876).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 876, 913, 940.

q: בן 87 הוא חולה נוטה למות עקב אי ספיקת לב סופנית. בעבר חתם על מינוי ייפוי כוח לפי חוק החולה הנוטה למות. כעת הוא נמצא באשפוז במחלקה קרדיולוגית בשל סינקופה המיוחס לחסם הולכתי וזקוק להכנסת קוצב. מי קובע אם החולה כשיר לקבל החלטה או שיש להפעיל את מיופה הכוח?
o: רק גריאטר יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק החולה הנוטה למות
רופא מומחה לפי בחירת החולה ( בזמן שמילא את הטופס) יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק החולה הנוטה למות
רק אם הרופא האחראי הוא גריאטר או פסיכיאטר, הוא יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות
כל רופא שהוגדר כרופא אחראי יכול להוציא מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק זה
explanation:
התשובה הרשמית היא **הרופא האחראי**: הוא מוסמך להוציא חולה מחזקת כשרות בהחלטה רפואית מנומקת ומתועדת, לאחר ההתייעצות הנדרשת (סעיף 7).

**א. רק גריאטר יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק החולה הנוטה למות.** שגויה, החוק אינו מייחד את הסמכות לגריאטר. הקובע הוא מינוי כרופא אחראי, ולא התמחות בגריאטריה (סעיפים 3, 7; עמ׳ PDF 4, 6).
**ב. רופא מומחה לפי בחירת החולה ( בזמן שמילא את הטופס) יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק החולה הנוטה למות.** שגויה, החוק מגדיר מי הוא הרופא האחראי בפועל; בחירה מראש של רופא בטופס ייפוי כוח אינה המסלול להקניית סמכות זו (סעיפים 3, 7; עמ׳ PDF 4, 6).
**ג. רק אם הרופא האחראי הוא גריאטר או פסיכיאטר, הוא יכול להחליט על הוצאה מחזקת הכשרות.** שגויה, התמחות בגריאטריה או בפסיכיאטריה אינה תנאי בסעיף. יש להתייעץ עם המטפלים והרופאים הרלוונטיים או מומחים, ובמידת האפשר עם הרופא האישי (סעיף 7; עמ׳ PDF 6).
**ד. כל רופא שהוגדר כרופא אחראי יכול להוציא מחזקת הכשרות על פי חוק זה.** נכונה, באשפוז זהו מנהל מחלקה או יחידה המטפל בחולה, או רופא מומחה שמונה לכך בידי הגורם המוסמך. לכן גם הרופא האחראי במחלקה הקרדיולוגית יכול לקבוע זאת. ההחלטה חייבת להיות מנומקת ומתועדת לאחר התייעצות. נקודת המוצא היא חזקת כשרות לאדם שמלאו לו 17 שנים ושלא הוכרז פסול דין, לקבל החלטות מתוך הבנה, שיקול דעת ורצון חופשי (סעיפים 3, 6–7; עמ׳ PDF 4, 6).

מקור: חוק החולה הנוטה למות, תשס״ו–2005, סעיפים 3, 6–7, עמ׳ PDF 4, 6.
ref: חוק החולה הנוטה למות; section not specified
chapterTitle: DECISION MAKING AND ADVANCE CARE PLANNING: WHAT MATTERS MOST

q: An 84-year-old woman receives several recommendations after comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA). After six weeks of monitoring, progress toward the agreed goals is below expectations. Her daughter reports reduced motivation. Which next step follows the CGA process?
o: Continue the existing plan with a longer observation period
Return care to the primary physician with the existing plan
Reassess the patient and revise the plan through team discussion
Increase the frequency of interventions within the existing plan
explanation:
**Revising the treatment plan** is part of CGA when progress falls short of expectations. Reassessment should include the patient because goals or readiness to change may have shifted, and revisions require further monitoring (p. 130).
"If progress is not proceeding according to expectations, the team may need to reevaluate the patient and resume the team discussion." (p. 130).
"Again, engaging the patient is important as readiness to change or the patient’s goals may have changed." (p. 130).

**A. Continue the existing plan with a longer observation period.** Wrong, extending observation leaves the unexpected lack of progress unexamined; the source calls for reconsidering the patient and plan in this situation (p. 130).
**B. Return care to the primary physician with the existing plan.** Wrong, returning care with the existing plan does not address the unmet goals or changed readiness that prompted reassessment (p. 130).
**C. Reassess the patient and revise the plan through team discussion.** Correct, reevaluation and renewed team discussion allow recommendations and implementation to be adjusted to the patient's current goals and readiness (p. 130).
**D. Increase the frequency of interventions within the existing plan.** Wrong, more frequent delivery preserves the same recommendations without assessing whether those recommendations or goals need revision (p. 130).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 130.
ref: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 130, Revising the treatment plan
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 130, Revising the treatment plan

q: A 90-year-old man with severe COPD on home oxygen, heart failure, and BPH presents with acute urinary retention. Catheterization drains 1.2 liters. His eGFR is 28 mL/min/1.73 m², and he takes furosemide 40 mg twice daily, metoprolol, and finasteride. His urologist proposes GreenLight laser photovaporization (PVP). Which comparison with TURP is supported by Hazzard when discussing the procedure?
o: PVP provides a tissue specimen for pathological examination after vaporization
PVP has lower transfusion rates in patients at high bleeding risk
PVP requires longer catheterization and hospitalization than TURP in the cited trial
PVP has higher reoperation requirements than TURP in the cited multicenter trial
explanation:
**GreenLight PVP** vaporizes prostatic tissue and provides coagulation. Hazzard describes lower transfusion rates than TURP and consideration of PVP for high-bleeding-risk patients; this is a procedural comparison, not proof that one operation is safest for this particular patient (p. 569).
"due to lower transfusion rates compared to TURP and good safety outcomes reported in this population." (p. 569).

**A. PVP provides a tissue specimen for pathological examination after vaporization.** Wrong, the source states that vaporization leaves no tissue for pathological examination (p. 569).
**B. PVP has lower transfusion rates in patients at high bleeding risk.** Correct, this is the comparative bleeding advantage and clinical consideration described (p. 569).
**C. PVP requires longer catheterization and hospitalization than TURP in the cited trial.** Wrong, the cited trial reports shorter catheterization and hospital stay with PVP (p. 569).
**D. PVP has higher reoperation requirements than TURP in the cited multicenter trial.** Wrong, the cited multicenter trial reports a similar overall need for reoperation, not a higher requirement (p. 569).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 569.

q: After removal of an indwelling catheter, an older patient has persistent frequency, nocturia, and urinary leakage. His medicines were recently changed. According to Hazzard's bladder-retraining protocol, what should precede a trial of a bladder relaxant?
o: Start a bladder relaxant before investigating possible medication effects
Evaluate reversible causes and determine the postvoid residual volume
Attribute the symptoms to bladder disease before reviewing the medicines
Base treatment on voiding frequency before checking bladder emptying
explanation:
**Bladder retraining after catheter removal** includes checking postvoid residual volume when voiding is frequent. If frequency and nocturia persist, the protocol calls for excluding reversible causes, including medication effects, and considering a bladder relaxant when residuals are low (p. 711).
"Perform postvoid residual determination to ensure the patient is completely emptying the bladder." (p. 711).

**A. Start a bladder relaxant before investigating possible medication effects.** Wrong, the protocol first calls for excluding reversible causes, explicitly including medication effects (p. 711).
**B. Evaluate reversible causes and determine the postvoid residual volume.** Correct, this checks both adequate bladder emptying and potentially reversible causes before the proposed drug trial (p. 711).
**C. Attribute the symptoms to bladder disease before reviewing the medicines.** Wrong, medication effects are a listed reversible cause and must be considered in the stated sequence (p. 711).
**D. Base treatment on voiding frequency before checking bladder emptying.** Wrong, frequency should prompt a postvoid residual determination to assess complete emptying (p. 711).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 711.

q: גבר בן 80, המוגדר חסר ישע, מאושפז שוב עקב החמרה באי־ספיקת לב. בנו אחראי למתן התרופות. אי־התאמות בטיפול ופחד של המטופל מבנו מעוררים חשד להזנחה בידי האחראי עליו. לצד בדיקה רפואית, הגנה ועירוב עובד סוציאלי, מהו סף חובת הדיווח לפקיד סעד או למשטרה המתואר בנוהל?
o: יסוד סביר לחשוב שנעברה עבירה בידי האחראי
ממצא חד־משמעי בחקירה המוכיח עבירה בידי האחראי
הודאה מתועדת של האחראי בביצוע העבירה המדוברת
הסכמה חתומה של המשפחה להעברת החשד לרשויות
explanation:
חובת הדיווח המתוארת בנוהל מבוססת על **יסוד סביר לחשוב שנעברה עבירה** בחסר ישע בידי האחראי עליו, ולא על הכרעה שיפוטית. יש לדווח בהקדם האפשרי, ובמקביל לבצע בירור רפואי וסוציאלי ולדאוג להגנת הנפגע. החשד בשאלה מצריך בירור; אין בו כשלעצמו קביעה שהבן ביצע עבירה (עמ׳ 2, 6).
"היה להם יסוד סביר לחשוב כי נעברה עבירה בקטין או בחסר ישע בידי האחראי עליו, חובה עליהם לדווח על כך בהקדם האפשרי לפקיד הסעד או למשטרה." (עמ׳ 2).

**א. יסוד סביר לחשוב שנעברה עבירה בידי האחראי.** נכונה, זהו הרף שהנוהל מצטט לחובת הדיווח. הוא מאפשר פנייה לרשויות כבר על בסיס חשד מבוסס, כדי שיבררו ויגנו על המטופל (עמ׳ 2, 6).
**ב. ממצא חד־משמעי בחקירה המוכיח עבירה בידי האחראי.** שגויה, דרישה לממצא חקירתי חד־משמעי מעכבת את הדיווח מעבר לרף שבנוהל. החובה היא לדווח בהקדם על יסוד סביר לחשוב שנעברה עבירה, לפני השלמת הוכחתה (עמ׳ 2).
**ג. הודאה מתועדת של האחראי בביצוע העבירה המדוברת.** שגויה, הודאה אינה תנאי בנוהל. חובת הדיווח יכולה להתקיים על סמך הממצאים והחשד המבוסס גם כשהאחראי מכחיש את הפגיעה (עמ׳ 2).
**ד. הסכמה חתומה של המשפחה להעברת החשד לרשויות.** שגויה, החובה החוקית המובאת בנוהל אינה מותנית באישור המשפחה. רף הדיווח הוא החשד המבוסס לעבירה בידי האחראי, ולכן חתימה משפחתית אינה מחליפה אותו (עמ׳ 2).

מקור: משרד הבריאות, נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות, עמ׳ 2, 6, סעיפים 1.2, 8, 9.
ref: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות · PDF pp.2, 6, sections 1.2, 8–10
label: Source: נוהל טיפול בזקנים נפגעי התעמרות · PDF pp.2, 6, sections 1.2, 8–10

q: An 80-year-old woman with severe knee osteoarthritis has recurrent pain rated 7/10 that limits shopping. A course of three hyaluronic acid injections six months ago initially helped. She has heart failure with an ejection fraction of 35% and stage 3b CKD, and takes furosemide, lisinopril, and carvedilol. Examination shows an effusion and crepitus. She is reluctant to undergo the knee replacement recommended by her surgeon. Which injectable option has evidence for symptomatic relief in Hazzard, while the other choices are described as lacking clear benefit or remaining experimental?
o: Intra-articular injection using hyaluronic acid
Intra-articular injection using a glucocorticoid
Intra-articular injection using platelet-rich plasma
Intra-articular injection using mesenchymal stem cells
explanation:
**Intra-articular glucocorticoids** have evidence for symptomatic relief in osteoarthritis. Hazzard states: "Intra-articular glucocorticoid (eg, methylprednisolone, triamcinolone) injections can significantly relieve pain due to OA." (p. 788). The benefit may be short-lived; the chapter distinguishes this evidence from the lack of clear benefit for hyaluronic acid after addressing study bias and the experimental status of platelet-rich plasma and mesenchymal stem-cell therapy (p. 789).

**A. Intra-articular injection using hyaluronic acid.** Wrong, the chapter reports no clear benefit in meta-analyses accounting for study bias. The patient’s initial subjective benefit does not change the evidence distinction asked for, although the source allows an individual trial after other options fail (p. 789; application).
**B. Intra-articular injection using a glucocorticoid.** Correct, the chapter supports pain relief from glucocorticoid injections and specifically describes efficacy in knee or hip osteoarthritis, matching the symptomatic option asked for (pp. 788–789).
**C. Intra-articular injection using platelet-rich plasma.** Wrong, the chapter describes platelet-rich plasma as experimental; it is not the option with the established symptomatic evidence stated here (p. 789).
**D. Intra-articular injection using mesenchymal stem cells.** Wrong, the chapter also describes mesenchymal stem-cell therapy as experimental, rather than the established symptomatic injection asked for (p. 789).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th edition, pp. 788, 789.

q: A 77-year-old woman with HFpEF (EF 58%), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and biopsy-proven transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis has NYHA class II symptoms despite furosemide 40 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily. Echocardiography shows LV wall thickening and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. Which treatment is the TTR stabilizer described in Hazzard as reducing mortality versus placebo in ATTR-ACT?
o: Metoprolol as the TTR-stabilizing treatment
Spironolactone as the TTR-stabilizing treatment
Tafamidis as the TTR-stabilizing treatment
Sacubitril/valsartan as the TTR-stabilizing treatment
explanation:
**Tafamidis** stabilizes transthyretin and was studied in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis. In ATTR-ACT it was associated with lower all-cause mortality than placebo and reduced cardiovascular hospitalization risk; this is evidence for a disease-specific treatment, not a head-to-head ranking of these drugs (p. 1188).
"For patients diagnosed with transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis, tafamidis, a TTR stabilizer" (p. 1188).

**A. Metoprolol as the TTR-stabilizing treatment.** Wrong, Metoprolol is not the agent identified as the TTR stabilizer in the cited trial (p. 1188).
**B. Spironolactone as the TTR-stabilizing treatment.** Wrong, Spironolactone is not the TTR stabilizer identified in ATTR-ACT (p. 1188).
**C. Tafamidis as the TTR-stabilizing treatment.** Correct, Tafamidis is explicitly identified as the TTR stabilizer with the stated placebo-controlled mortality result (p. 1188).
**D. Sacubitril/valsartan as the TTR-stabilizing treatment.** Wrong, the page discusses sacubitril/valsartan separately as an ARNI; the TTR-stabilizer evidence is for tafamidis (p. 1188).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1188.

q: An older man with hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction is being considered for a beta-blocker. Which consideration supports its use according to Hazzard?
o: Secondary prevention after a previous myocardial infarction
Its role as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension
Its role in reducing peripheral vascular resistance
Its role in preventing adverse metabolic effects
explanation:
**Beta-blocker selection** in older adults depends on a compelling indication. Hazzard reserves these drugs for indications including "secondary prevention for those patients who have had prior myocardial infarction" (p. 1226). It does not recommend beta-blocker monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension in older patients (p. 1226).

**A. Secondary prevention after a previous myocardial infarction.** Correct, previous myocardial infarction is a stated compelling indication, so the drug has a role beyond treatment of uncomplicated hypertension (p. 1226).
**B. Its role as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension.** Wrong, Hazzard explicitly states that beta-blockers are not an appropriate monotherapy choice for older patients with uncomplicated hypertension (p. 1226).
**C. Its role in reducing peripheral vascular resistance.** Wrong, the table lists a possible increase in peripheral vascular resistance as a disadvantage, so the proposed vascular effect is not the stated reason to choose this class (p. 1226).
**D. Its role in preventing adverse metabolic effects.** Wrong, metabolic abnormalities are listed as a disadvantage of beta-blockers, rather than a benefit supporting selection (p. 1226).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1226.

q: A 77-year-old woman has ulcerative colitis in remission on mesalamine 800 mg three times daily. Over 3 months, she has developed straining and a bowel movement every 4 days. She also takes weekly alendronate and vitamin D, and recently started amitriptyline 10 mg for peripheral neuropathy. There is no abdominal tenderness. Which mechanism explains the constipating effect of an anticholinergic medication?
o: Enhanced smooth-muscle contraction through muscarinic stimulation
Reduced smooth-muscle contraction through antimuscarinic activity
Increased stool water through chloride-channel activation
Increased propulsive activity through serotonin-receptor stimulation
explanation:
**Anticholinergic medications** reduce gut smooth-muscle contractility through an antimuscarinic effect. This gives a mechanism for drug-related constipation without establishing that a medication is the sole cause of this patient's symptoms (p. 1358).
"Anticholinergic medications reduce contractility of the smooth muscle of the gut via an antimuscarinic effect at acetylcholine receptor sites" (p. 1358).
"inducing secretion of fluid and electrolytes through the activation of the type-2 chloride channels in the intestinal apical cell membrane." (p. 1377).

**A. Enhanced smooth-muscle contraction through muscarinic stimulation.** Wrong, the source describes reduced contractility through antimuscarinic activity, not enhanced contraction through stimulation (p. 1358).
**B. Reduced smooth-muscle contraction through antimuscarinic activity.** Correct, reduced gut contractility is the mechanism stated for anticholinergic medications and explains their constipating effect (p. 1358).
**C. Increased stool water through chloride-channel activation.** Wrong, chloride-channel activation induces intestinal secretion in the secretagogue discussion; it does not describe antimuscarinic reduction in contractility (pp. 1358, 1377).
**D. Increased propulsive activity through serotonin-receptor stimulation.** Wrong, serotonin 5-HT4 agonists stimulate gastrointestinal motility; this is a prokinetic action, unlike the anticholinergic effect asked about (pp. 1358, 1377).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1358, 1377.

q: An older man with Alzheimer disease develops confusion, dry mouth, and constipation after starting oxybutynin. Which explanation is consistent with the drug effects listed in Hazzard?
o: A cholinergic drug effect involving cognition and gastrointestinal function
An anticholinergic drug effect involving cognition and gastrointestinal function
A cholinergic drug effect associated with improvement in constipation
An anticholinergic drug effect associated with improvement in delirium
explanation:
**Oxybutynin** has anticholinergic adverse effects that include dry mouth, delirium, and constipation. These effects make the medication a plausible contributor to the symptoms in the stem; identifying compatibility does not establish it as the sole cause (p. 712).
"Anticholinergic (dry mouth, blurry vision, elevated intraocular pressure, delirium, constipation)" (p. 712).

**A. A cholinergic drug effect involving cognition and gastrointestinal function.** Wrong, the table identifies anticholinergic rather than cholinergic effects (p. 712).
**B. An anticholinergic drug effect involving cognition and gastrointestinal function.** Correct, the stated cognitive and gastrointestinal symptoms are compatible with the listed anticholinergic adverse effects (p. 712).
**C. A cholinergic drug effect associated with improvement in constipation.** Wrong, Oxybutynin is anticholinergic and constipation is an adverse effect, not the described therapeutic response (p. 712).
**D. An anticholinergic drug effect associated with improvement in delirium.** Wrong, the table lists delirium as an adverse effect rather than an expected improvement (p. 712).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 712.

q: A 78-year-old man with CLL takes ibrutinib 420 mg/day. He also has hypertension treated with lisinopril 10 mg and stage 3a CKD (eGFR 45); he takes aspirin 81 mg. He presents with three weeks of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea and five days of dark stools. He is pale, with BP 128/78, heart rate 96, no orthostatic changes, and no lymphadenopathy. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL (baseline 11.2), MCV 82, platelets 165,000, WBC 42,000 with 85% lymphocytes, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.4). He has received one unit of packed red cells and is hemodynamically stable. Which statement about ibrutinib is relevant to reviewing his bleeding risk?
o: It reduces bleeding propensity, so concurrent antiplatelet therapy is reassuring
It increases bleeding propensity, requiring antiplatelet risk-benefit review
It increases bleeding propensity, making concurrent antiplatelet therapy protective
It reduces bleeding propensity, making a medication contribution less concerning
explanation:
**Ibrutinib-associated bleeding** is a medication-safety concern in the source (p. 1497). Hazzard describes "propensity toward bleeding" and calls for risk-benefit consideration in patients requiring antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment (p. 1497). Applied to this vignette, that supports reviewing the drug combination; it does not prove the cause of the anemia or establish a complete acute-management sequence.

**A. It reduces bleeding propensity, so concurrent antiplatelet therapy is reassuring.** Wrong, ibrutinib is associated with bleeding propensity rather than a protective effect, so the proposed reassurance is misplaced (p. 1497).
**B. It increases bleeding propensity, requiring antiplatelet risk-benefit review.** Correct, the source’s bleeding warning and antiplatelet risk-benefit consideration are relevant to reviewing this patient’s medications (p. 1497).
**C. It increases bleeding propensity, making concurrent antiplatelet therapy protective.** Wrong, the source calls for risk-benefit consideration with antiplatelet treatment; it does not describe the combination as protecting against bleeding (p. 1497).
**D. It reduces bleeding propensity, making a medication contribution less concerning.** Wrong, the drug’s documented bleeding propensity supports attention to a medication contribution rather than reassurance on this basis (p. 1497).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1497.

q: בת 80 הגיעה למרפאה למעקב של צפיפות העצם. מטופלת ב- ALENDRONATE 70 מ"ג פעם בשבוע מזה 7 שנים בשל אוסטאופורוזיס. בבדיקת צפיפות העצם T-SCORE -2.22.בצוואר ירך ימין. ללא היסטוריה של שברים, ללא ירידה בגובה, ללא היסטוריה משפחתית של שברים בירך. מה מהאפשרויות הבאות היא הניהול המתאים ביותר לבריאות העצם שלה ?
o: להמשך טיפול ב- ALENDRONATE
להמשיך טיפול ב- ALENDRONATE ולהוסיף טיפול ב- TERIPARATIDE (FORTEO)
להפסיק טיפול ב- ALENDRONATE
להפסיק טיפול ב- ALENDRONATE ולתת טיפול ב- TERIPARATIDE (FORTEO)
explanation:
After prolonged treatment, reassess fracture risk and consider a **bisphosphonate holiday** when risk is low or moderate. Duration of treatment or bone density alone does not automatically determine the decision (p. 777).

**A. Continue alendronate.** Wrong, continuation may suit high fracture risk but is not the official choice here. Future risk must be assessed before deciding, as the retained note below explains (p. 777).
**B. Continue alendronate and add teriparatide.** Wrong, anabolic therapy is directed mainly toward very high fracture risk or multiple fractures; the stem does not establish that basis for escalation (p. 777).
**C. Discontinue alendronate.** Correct, the official choice. A holiday may be considered after prolonged therapy in low- or moderate-risk patients, with risk reassessment rather than automatic discontinuation (p. 777).
**D. Discontinue alendronate and start teriparatide.** Wrong, this escalates to anabolic therapy, which the page directs toward very high fracture risk or multiple fractures not described here (p. 777).

Official answer: ג. A bisphosphonate holiday can be considered after prolonged treatment if the overall assessment indicates low or moderate fracture risk; reassess future risk rather than inferring safety from the T-score alone (p. 777).

Balance future fracture risk against the benefits and disadvantages of prolonged therapy before deciding on a holiday (p. 777).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 777.

q: בת 75 אובחנה עם היצרות חמורה של המסתם האאורטאלי לאחר בירור של כאבים בחזה. איזה מהשיקולים הבאים בבחירת הטיפול המתאים בין Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) ל- Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement (SAVR) הוא הנכון ומדוע?
o: ביצוע TAVR בנוכחות סימני אי ספיקת לב כי צפוי שיפור משמעותי יותר בתסמינים
ביצוע SAVR לאחר הקרנות לבית החזה בעבר כי יש סיכוי נמוך יותר להתערבות חוזרת
ביצוע TAVR אם יש ריבוי מחלות רקע כי מפחית סיכון להשתלת קוצב
ביצוע SAVR אם יש מחלה קורונרית תלת כלית כי ניתן לבצע 2 התערבויות בבת אחת
explanation:
The choice of **SAVR or TAVR** depends on anatomy, comorbidities and treatment risk. Concomitant coronary artery disease is a factor favoring surgical replacement (p. 1153, Table 75-3).

**A. TAVR with heart-failure signs because it gives greater symptom improvement.** Wrong, both approaches improve symptoms, quality of life and survival. The table does not favor TAVR on the basis of greater improvement in heart-failure symptoms (p. 1153).
**B. SAVR after previous chest irradiation because repeat intervention is less likely.** Wrong, prior chest irradiation is a factor favoring TAVR, so it is not the proposed reason for choosing surgery (p. 1153).
**C. TAVR with multiple comorbidities because it reduces pacemaker implantation.** Wrong, severe comorbidity can favor TAVR, but the pacemaker rationale is wrong: pacemaker implantation risk is higher with TAVR (p. 1153).
**D. SAVR with three-vessel coronary disease so both procedures can be performed together.** Correct, concomitant coronary disease favors surgery. Application to this case: when surgical revascularization is needed, it can be combined with valve replacement as the option proposes (p. 1153).

When significant three-vessel coronary disease requires surgical revascularization (CABG), combining bypass surgery and valve replacement in one operation supports SAVR. This is the clinical application of the table’s concomitant-coronary-disease criterion (p. 1153).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1153.
